questions.question: Where does log-based CDC normally read changes?
options: From a trigger-maintained audit table the application writes on every change
From the database's transaction log, which already records every committed change
From a materialized view the database refreshes after each committed transaction
From the query planner's statistics, which track how often each row is modified

questions.question: What is a core advantage of log-based CDC over table polling?
options: It removes the need to take an initial snapshot of the rows that already exist
It runs through ordinary SQL credentials without replication privileges
It observes committed deletes and every intermediate change between polls
It guarantees the consumer can never fall behind the source's log retention

questions.question: Why can polling with updated_at greater than the last timestamp lose rows?
options: Rows can share the cursor timestamp, or commit after the cursor has passed them
The source clock drifts, so timestamps written by replicas are always rejected
Any row updated twice within one interval is filtered out as a duplicate change
Indexes on timestamp columns go stale, so recent rows are skipped under load

questions.question: How can query-based CDC capture deletes reliably?
options: Poll more frequently so a deleted row is observed before it disappears
Compare each poll against the previous poll and treat absences as deletes
Read a monotonically increasing ID, which stops advancing once a row is gone
Use soft-delete flags, a separate deletion log, or a periodic full comparison

questions.question: What composite polling cursor avoids skipping rows that share an update timestamp?
options: `(updated_at, primary_key)`, compared lexicographically so ties still advance
`(updated_at, row_version)`, resetting the version counter on every poll run
`(primary_key, updated_at)`, so the scan follows the table's clustering order
`(updated_at, poll_number)`, which records which run first observed the row

questions.question: How should an initial snapshot hand off to a log stream without a gap?
options: Snapshot the table first, then begin reading the log from the position reached at the end
Record a log position, take a snapshot consistent with it, then replay from that position
Run both concurrently and let the snapshot overwrite any change it disagrees with
Pause writes to the source until the snapshot completes, then start the log reader

questions.topic: Ordering and Schema Changes in CDC Streams
questions.question: What is normally safer than a wall-clock timestamp for CDC ordering?
options: The time the consumer acknowledged the event to the message broker
The commit timestamp assigned by the source database's primary node
A source log sequence number or per-row version position
The order in which the connector's worker threads finished decoding

questions.topic: Ordering and Schema Changes in CDC Streams
questions.question: What is needed for a consumer to decode events across schema changes?
options: A guarantee that producers only ever append fields to the end of the record
A single reader schema that every producer is required to conform to
A replay of the full history whenever the writer's schema is altered
A schema identifier on each event plus reader logic that maps writer to reader

questions.topic: Ordering and Schema Changes in CDC Streams
questions.question: How can a latest-state sink prevent an older event from overwriting a newer one?
options: Store the last applied source version per key and reject anything not newer
Buffer each key's events briefly and apply them in arrival order once settled
Partition the topic by primary key so every event for a key is strictly ordered
Compare the incoming payload against the stored row and skip identical writes

questions.topic: Ordering and Schema Changes in CDC Streams
questions.question: Why should a delete tombstone retain its source version through the replay window?
options: So the connector can measure how far behind the source retention it has fallen
So a delayed older update cannot be applied and resurrect the deleted row
So the sink can restore the row if the delete is later found to be erroneous
So downstream consumers can distinguish a hard delete from a soft delete flag

questions.topic: Ordering and Schema Changes in CDC Streams
questions.question: Why does per-key ordering not guarantee an atomic account transfer?
options: The debit and credit are written by separate connectors with independent cursors
Transaction boundaries are stripped from the log before the connector reads them
The debit and credit live on different keys, so each can become visible alone
Per-key ordering only holds within one partition, and a transfer spans two of them

questions.topic: Ordering and Schema Changes in CDC Streams
questions.question: What is the safe rollout for a breaking field replacement?
options: Publish the new field, cut consumers over in one release, then drop the old field
Keep the field name and type but change its meaning, then announce the change
Drop the old field first so no consumer can keep depending on it during migration
Add the new field, dual-publish both, migrate and backfill consumers, then retire the old
